analysis.one_liner: Moves the consumer financial protection bureau from the Federal Reserve into the Treasury Department.
analysis.headline: The bill to move the consumer bureau under Treasury died in a House subcommittee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would relocate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — the watchdog created after the 2008 financial crisis to police mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer loans — from its independent home inside the Federal Reserve to the Treasury Department, a cabinet agency under the president. It would also cut the bureau's ties to the Federal Reserve's retirement plans. Supporters said this would make the bureau more accountable; critics said placing a consumer watchdog inside a cabinet agency would expose it to political pressure from the industries it regulates.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, lenders, and other financial companies regulated by the bureau would benefit from a weaker, more politically exposed regulator. Moving the bureau under Treasury and eliminating its independence features would make its rules and enforcement easier to influence through the administration of the day. Ordinary consumers lose the strong independent watchdog that polices fees, lending practices, and financial fraud on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Transfers the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection from the Federal Reserve System to the Department of the Treasury, replacing the Federal Reserve Board's oversight role with the Treasury Secretary's [S2, S3].
Prohibits the Treasury Secretary from interfering with the bureau's autonomy, while cutting the bureau's participation in the Federal Reserve's retirement and thrift plans [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, who rely on the bureau to police predatory lending, credit card fees, mortgage abuses, and financial fraud. A bureau housed inside a cabinet department is easier for the industries it regulates to influence through the White House of the day.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of the CFPB's original design argued its independence — funded through the Federal Reserve rather than congressional appropriations and housed outside the administration — was intended to shield it from lobbying pressure by the financial industry; moving it into Treasury would expose it to that pressure [S2].
Supporters' good-faith case: a bureau inside the Federal Reserve answers to no elected official, and placing it in Treasury would subject it to ordinary executive accountability [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument has some force, but the practical effect of the bill would have been to weaken the primary regulator that polices consumer lending on ordinary people's behalf, for the benefit of the firms being regulated. The bill attracted no cosponsors and never moved, so the design concerns were never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, sat there without a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 8, 2011 by Rep. Randy Neugebauer with no cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1, S4, S5].
Referred on March 23, 2011 to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it stayed without any further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept the consumer bureau's independent structure intact; no financial-industry relief was enacted through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and the consumer bureau's structure

for.name: Rep. Randy Neugebauer
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to move the consumer bureau into Treasury; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or a floor vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from March 2011 onward with no further action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and consumer financial firms
industries.note: These firms are the CFPB's regulated subjects; moving the bureau into Treasury and weakening its independence would make its rules and enforcement easier to soften through the administration of the day. Consumers would bear the cost through weaker policing of fees and lending practices.
The bill strips the Federal Reserve of its role housing the bureau and removes the bureau from the Fed's retirement and thrift plans.
